title: Thomson Reuters, RELX, and Wolters Stocks Crushed After Anthropic Debuts Claude Legal Plug-In
author: Rob Hales

dom.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows

st.t: Model providers: Suppliers now compete for workflows
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s nuanced position: Anthropic’s direct legal-technology entry creates competitive and growth risk, but the sell-off shows perceived disruption rather than realised displacement. It also reinforces the continued importance of specialist incumbents’ legal-research moats and concludes that Claude’s plug-in is not yet a sufficient threat to revise valuations.
qs: Claude’s legal plug-in is the first direct push into legal technology by a major large language model provider, broadening the disruption story previously driven by AI-native startups like Harvey.
- Importantly, the plug-in has nothing to do with legal research, which is the core value proposition and wide-moat foundation of Thomson and RELX’s legal businesses.

kp.k: Claude launch intensifies legal technology disruption fears
kp.d: Morningstar reports that on Feb. 3, in this 2026 analysis, Thomson Reuters, RELX and Wolters Kluwer shares fell 16%, 14% and 13%, respectively, after Anthropic released its Claude legal plug-in. The author characterises this as the first direct legal technology push by a major large language model provider, extending a disruption narrative previously driven by AI-native startups such as Harvey and weighing on these stocks since summer 2025.
qs: On Feb. 3, Thomson Reuters (TRI), RELX (REL), and Wolters Kluwer’s (WKL) stocks fell 16%, 14%, and 13%, respectively, after Anthropic released a legal plug-in for its Claude product.
This is the latest turn in the artificial intelligence disruption narrative that’s weighed on these stocks since summer 2025.
Claude’s legal plug-in is the first direct push into legal technology by a major large language model provider, broadening the disruption story previously driven by AI-native startups like Harvey.

kp.k: In-house AI assistance could reduce external provider growth
kp.d: The plug-in targets corporate legal teams with assistance for contract reviews, legal briefings and templated responses. Morningstar identifies a prospective risk to legal technology providers' growth if users can perform more work in-house; the document does not report measured adoption, productivity gains or actual substitution.
qs: Claude’s legal plug-in is targeting in-house legal teams to aid with tasks like contract reviews, legal briefings, and templated responses.
This represents the new AI assistant market.
The risk is lower growth as users are able to do more in-house rather than outsource to legal technology providers.

kp.k: Legal research remains distinct from the plug-in’s scope
kp.d: Morningstar argues that the plug-in does not address legal research, which it identifies as the core value proposition and foundation of the wide moats of Thomson Reuters' and RELX's legal businesses. This distinction qualifies the perceived competitive threat from the new assistant.
qs: Importantly, the plug-in has nothing to do with legal research, which is the core value proposition and wide-moat foundation of Thomson and RELX’s legal businesses.

kp.k: Morningstar retains positive AI growth assumptions and valuations
kp.d: Morningstar maintains wide-moat assessments and fair value estimates for all three companies, judging their shares significantly undervalued. Its valuation assumptions still treat generative AI as positive for legal growth, and it regards the plug-in as insufficiently clear a threat to revise estimates yet. The author questions the magnitude of the sell-off, arguing that these stocks had already derated sharply as AI expectations shifted from upside to overhang; these are investment judgments rather than demonstrated future outcomes.
qs: We maintain our wide moats and fair value estimates for all three firms. At current levels, all three stocks look significantly undervalued.
A drawdown of this magnitude implies the market was still pricing in meaningful AI-driven upside in legal, which doesn’t make sense.
These stocks have already derated sharply over the past year as this story turned from upside to overhang.
Our fair value estimates assume generative AI is positive for legal growth at these companies.
We don’t see this as a clear enough threat to change our estimates yet.

kp.k: Legal earnings exposure makes Thomson most vulnerable
kp.d: Morningstar identifies Thomson Reuters as most exposed to the threat because legal accounts for 45% of its EBIT, compared with 10%-13% for RELX and Wolters. These figures describe earnings exposure, not estimated AI-driven losses. The author expects Thomson's Feb. 5 earnings report to provide further information about the potential risk.
qs: Thomson is most at risk, with 45% of EBIT from legal, while RELX and Wolters only generate 10%-13% of EBIT from legal.
Thomson will report earnings on Feb. 5, which should help illuminate the potential risk of this new threat.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hales characterises Claude’s legal plug-in as a major LLM provider’s first direct entry into legal technology, expanding competition beyond AI-native startups.
pts.d: Writing for Morningstar, Rob Hales says Anthropic’s entry broadens the AI disruption narrative previously driven by companies such as Harvey. The plug-in targets the AI assistant market for in-house legal work, including contract reviews, briefings and templated responses.

pts.k: Hales identifies a risk that AI assistants reduce legal technology providers’ growth by enabling users to perform more work in-house.
pts.d: This is framed as a potential substitution effect, not as an observed reduction in purchases or revenue. The source specifically identifies legal technology providers as exposed; it does not report displacement of law firms or lawyer jobs.

pts.k: Hales distinguishes the assistant threat from legal research and maintains Morningstar’s expectation that generative AI supports incumbents’ legal growth.
pts.d: Hales says the plug-in does not address legal research, which underpins Thomson Reuters’ and RELX’s competitive advantages. Morningstar retains its wide-moat assessments and fair value estimates for Thomson Reuters, RELX and Wolters Kluwer, judging the new threat insufficiently clear to revise them. Its valuation assumptions remain positive about generative AI’s contribution to legal growth, and it regards all three stocks as significantly undervalued at publication.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers product-scope descriptions, stock-price movements and legal earnings exposure, rather than measured evidence of AI productivity or revenue displacement.
pts.d: Hales reports one-day stock declines following the launch and interprets them as part of an existing disruption narrative. He supplies legal EBIT shares to distinguish company exposure. The growth-risk mechanism and positive growth outlook are analyst judgments or valuation assumptions; the article provides no adoption data, task-performance benchmarks, customer outcomes or quantified growth forecasts. Hales also interprets the size of the sell-off as implying that investors had still priced in meaningful AI upside.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The assessment concerns the February 3, 2026 launch and sell-off, with no specified horizon for the predicted growth effects.
pts.d: Hales situates the launch within disruption concerns weighing on these stocks since summer 2025. The lower-growth risk depends on users doing more work internally. The retained positive outlook is provisional: the current plug-in’s exclusion of legal research limits the identified threat, and Hales says the evidence is not clear enough to revise estimates yet. Thomson Reuters’ February 5 earnings release is identified as a near-term opportunity to clarify the risk.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified effects concern in-house legal teams, legal technology providers and investors, with Thomson Reuters described as the most exposed incumbent.
pts.d: In-house teams are the intended users of assistance with contracts, briefings and templated responses. Legal technology providers face a possible reduction in growth as more work remains internal. Thomson Reuters has greater company-level exposure through legal EBIT than RELX or Wolters Kluwer. Legal research is distinguished as the foundation of Thomson Reuters’ and RELX’s moats, outside the plug-in’s stated scope. Investors experienced the reported stock declines; the article makes no concrete claims about access to justice, staffing reductions or effects on individual legal consumers.
